overview: A good mulch job is mostly prep. We re-cut the bed edge so grass can't creep in and pull every weed by the root, because mulch hides weeds, it doesn't kill them. Then we loosen the top of the soil so water can reach the roots, and lay the mulch even, 1 to 1.5 inches deep, pulled back off stems and trunks.

We bring in bulk mulch by the yard for bigger jobs, so you pay for mulch and not packaging, and use bagged where access is tight. Shredded hardwood is the standard here. Cypress breaks down slower, dyed black or brown gives more contrast, and pine straw is there if that's your look. On a refresh we match what's already in the bed so it breaks down evenly.

process.title: Measure the beds
process.text: We walk the beds, measure the square footage and check how much of the old layer is left, so you only pay for what the beds need.

process.title: Edge and clean
process.text: Edges get re-cut, weeds come out by the root, and thin spots get topped up with soil where needed.

process.title: Loosen the soil
process.text: We break up the crusted top inch so rain gets down to the roots instead of running off.

process.title: Lay the mulch
process.text: Mulch goes down 1 to 1.5 inches deep, raked even and tapered off at stems and trunks.

process.title: Clean up
process.text: We blow off the walks and drive and haul away the debris.

price.note: The price follows how many yards of mulch and how many beds we're refreshing. A fall top-dress over a layer that's still there usually costs a fraction of a full install.

timing: The best window is late April through mid-May, right after the spring growth flush and before the heat shows up. The second is late September through October, when a thin top-dress goes down before the leaves drop and the first cold front comes through.

east_texas.title: Why we use half the mulch the calculator says
text: Every online calculator says three inches. That number comes from up north, where snow packs mulch down over the winter. We don't get snow loads here, and inches two and three just get buried where nobody sees them.

Three inches in East Texas sheds light rain like a tarp, holds heat and moisture against stems until they rot, and gives voles cover to eat roots all winter. So we prep the bed and lay 1 to 1.5 inches. For a 2,000 square foot bed, that's about 8 yards instead of 19. And we never put fabric under it. Mulch is supposed to turn into soil, and fabric stops that.

faq.q: How much does mulch installation cost in Longview, TX?
faq.a: Most mulch and bed refreshes run $600 to $2,400. Where you land depends on how many beds you have, how many yards of mulch they take, the type you pick, and how much edging and weed pulling they need. A fall top-dress over a layer that's still there costs less than a full install. We measure and send a written quote for free.

faq.q: How deep should mulch be in East Texas?
faq.a: About 1 to 1.5 inches over a prepped bed. Three inches sheds light rain, holds moisture against stems until they rot, and gives voles cover through the winter. For fresh mulch, divide your bed's square footage by 260 to get yards. A 2,000 square foot bed needs about 8 yards, not the 19 most calculators tell you to buy.

faq.q: What type of mulch is best for East Texas?
faq.a: Shredded hardwood is the standard for most beds here. It looks clean and breaks down into soil, which is part of the point. Cypress breaks down slower, cedar holds up well in our heat and humidity, and dyed black or brown gives more contrast. Pine straw works if you like the look. On a refresh, we match what's already in the bed.

faq.q: How often should mulch be refreshed?
faq.a: Most beds need a thin layer once a year, usually in spring. In fall, push a finger down through the mulch until you hit soil. If an inch is left, add an inch. Don't scrape the bed to bare dirt first. That old layer is turning into soil and feeding shallow-rooted shrubs like azaleas, hydrangeas and boxwood.

faq.q: Should I put landscape fabric under mulch?
faq.a: No. Mulch breaks down into soil, and on fabric that soil sits on top of the sheet, right where wind-blown weed seed lands and sprouts. The roots punch through, and pulling a weed tears up the fabric with it. Edge the bed and mulch at the right depth instead. Under river rock or gravel, fabric is the right call.
